subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Plague, Fire, Science & Witchcraft
subtitle: The Great Plague and Fire of London, the Scientific Revolution, and witch trials in early modern England.

data.targetWord: a serious infectious disease; in 1665 London suffered an outbreak of bubonic plague linked to bacteria spread by fleas on rats, causing tens of thousands of deaths

examples.en-GB: The Great Plague of 1665 killed around 100,000 people in London, with poorer communities suffering most severely.

data.targetWord: the early modern belief that disease was caused by bad or poisonous air, often linked to foul smells from waste and rotting material

examples.en-GB: People burned herbs to clean the air because they believed miasma — bad air — caused the plague.

data.targetWord: keeping people, ships, goods, or houses separate for a period of time to stop disease spreading to healthy people

examples.en-GB: Quarantine was used during the Great Plague: infected households had their doors locked and marked with a red cross.

data.targetWord: weekly records published in London listing numbers and causes of deaths, used by authorities to track the spread of plague

examples.en-GB: The Bills of Mortality allowed authorities to monitor how quickly the plague was spreading through different London parishes.

data.targetWord: a disease outbreak that spreads quickly through a community or region, affecting a large number of people at the same time

examples.en-GB: The Great Plague of 1665 was one of the deadliest epidemic outbreaks in English history.

data.targetWord: the devastating fire that began in Pudding Lane on 2 September 1666 and destroyed much of the old City of London, including thousands of houses and many churches

examples.en-GB: The Great Fire of London destroyed around 13,000 houses and old St Paul's Cathedral before being brought under control.

data.targetWord: a gap created by pulling down buildings to stop flames spreading — an emergency measure used during the Great Fire of London

examples.en-GB: Creating firebreaks by demolishing buildings was controversial because owners did not want their homes destroyed.

data.targetWord: a naval official and diarist who recorded detailed accounts of both the Great Plague and the Great Fire, providing valuable eyewitness evidence for historians

examples.en-GB: Samuel Pepys's diary entries about the Great Fire describe flames, chaos, people fleeing to the Thames, and the difficulty of creating firebreaks.

data.targetWord: the architect who helped redesign London after the Great Fire, most famously designing the new St Paul's Cathedral, which was completed in 1710

examples.en-GB: Christopher Wren designed over fifty churches after the Great Fire, creating a new architectural landscape for the City of London.

data.targetWord: the supposed use of magical powers, often believed in early modern times to be connected to a pact with the Devil, used to harm people, animals, or crops

examples.en-GB: Witchcraft accusations in early modern England often followed local quarrels, unexplained illness, or the death of livestock.

data.targetWord: a witch-finder active in East Anglia during 1645-1647 who called himself the 'Witchfinder General' and was responsible for many witchcraft accusations and executions

examples.en-GB: Matthew Hopkins was active during the English Civil War, a time of fear and instability that made communities more susceptible to witchcraft accusations.

data.targetWord: a scientific society founded in London in 1660 to promote observation, experiment, and shared evidence, with the motto 'Nullius in verba' — take nobody's word for it

examples.en-GB: The Royal Society encouraged members to share experimental results, challenging the older practice of accepting ancient authorities without question.

data.targetWord: a term used before the word 'scientist' became common, describing those who studied nature, the body, the heavens, and the physical world through observation and experiment

examples.en-GB: Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke were natural philosophers who used experiments and instruments to investigate the physical world.

data.targetWord: a broad change in the seventeenth century in which growing numbers of scholars began studying the natural world through observation, experiment, measurement, and shared evidence

examples.en-GB: The Scientific Revolution did not happen overnight — older beliefs such as miasma and astrology continued even as new experimental methods grew in influence.

data.targetWord: the modern scientific understanding that many diseases are caused by microorganisms such as bacteria and viruses — not developed until the nineteenth century

examples.en-GB: Without germ theory, seventeenth-century people could not understand that plague was spread by fleas on rats, leading to ineffective responses.

data.targetWord: the ancient medical theory that health depended on balancing four bodily substances — blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile — still widely used in early modern medicine

examples.en-GB: Doctors using the four humours theory might prescribe bleeding or purging to rebalance the body, treatments that were often useless or harmful.

data.targetWord: the street in the City of London where the Great Fire began on 2 September 1666, starting in the bakery of Thomas Farriner

examples.en-GB: The Great Fire began in Pudding Lane, but spread so rapidly due to timber buildings, narrow streets, and strong winds that it engulfed the entire city.

data.targetWord: a belief based on fear, tradition, or the supernatural rather than tested evidence — historians use this word carefully to avoid mocking past beliefs without understanding their context

examples.en-GB: Historians avoid simply calling witchcraft beliefs 'superstition' because that ignores the very real fears, local tensions, and social contexts that made accusations happen.

data.targetWord: a natural philosopher and Royal Society member who used observation and instruments to study nature, and helped survey London after the Great Fire

examples.en-GB: Robert Hooke used a microscope to study natural objects in extraordinary detail, helping to develop the practice of careful observation.

data.targetWord: actions taken by authorities or communities to protect people from disease, including cleaning streets, quarantine measures, and collecting death statistics

examples.en-GB: Public health responses to the plague, such as shutting up infected houses and publishing Bills of Mortality, show that authorities tried to act even without germ theory.

data.targetWord: a financial system in which people pay regular sums to be compensated if their property is destroyed by fire — developed more rapidly after the Great Fire of London

examples.en-GB: The Great Fire encouraged the growth of fire insurance in England, as people recognised the need for financial protection against future disasters.

data.targetWord: a supposed physical mark on the body used by early modern witch-finders as evidence that a person had made a pact with the Devil — an unreliable form of accusation

examples.en-GB: Witch-finders like Matthew Hopkins used searching for 'witch marks' as evidence, but this was based on superstition rather than any reliable proof.

data.targetWord: in the context of the Great Fire, this refers to the absence of firefighting capability rather than a modern blackout; the City lacked organised fire services, relying on buckets, hooks and demolition

examples.en-GB: London in 1666 had no organised fire service, so fighting the fire relied on buckets, water squirts, and the difficult decision to create firebreaks.

data.targetWord: a medicine or treatment made and used at home, often from herbs, food, drink, or traditional recipes, widely used because professional medicine was expensive and often ineffective

examples.en-GB: Household remedies were widely used during the plague because few people could afford a doctor, and medical treatments were often ineffective anyway.

data.targetWord: the conflict between Parliament and King Charles I from 1642 to 1651, which created political instability and social fear — contributing to the increase in witchcraft accusations in East Anglia

examples.en-GB: The social disruption of the English Civil War created an environment of fear and weak local authority in which Matthew Hopkins's witch-hunting could flourish.

data.sentence: The Great Plague of London occurred mainly in ____.
The Great Fire of London began in ____ Lane on 2 September 1666.
The belief that disease was caused by bad air or foul smells was called ____.
The Royal Society was founded in London in ____ to promote observation and experiment.
The architect ____ helped rebuild London after the Great Fire and designed the new St Paul's Cathedral.
Matthew Hopkins, the self-titled 'Witchfinder General', was mainly active in ____ during the 1640s.
Infected houses during the Great Plague were marked with a red ____ and had watchmen posted outside.
The Great Fire spread so quickly partly because many London buildings were made of ____.
The diarist ____ recorded detailed accounts of both the Great Plague and the Great Fire in London.
Witchcraft accusations in England were finally removed as a legal crime when witchcraft laws were repealed in ____.
The Royal Society's motto 'Nullius in verba' means roughly 'take nobody's ____ for it'.
The old medical theory of the four ____ claimed illness was caused by imbalance of blood, phlegm, and bile.
After the Great Fire, London buildings were required to use more ____ and stone instead of timber.
Many witchcraft accusations happened during the ____ War, a time of fear and political instability in England.
Weekly death records used to track plague in London were called Bills of ____.
Modern science understands that bubonic plague is spread by ____ carried by rats.

data.title: Put these events in chronological order
items: Matthew Hopkins witch-hunting in East Anglia (1645-1647)
Royal Society founded to promote experiment and observation (1660)
Great Plague of London kills tens of thousands (1665)
Great Fire of London destroys much of the City (1666)
Rebuilding of St Paul's Cathedral begins under Christopher Wren (1676)

data.title: Order the chain of causes and consequences for how the Great Fire spread
items: London has many timber-framed buildings with upper floors leaning over narrow streets
A dry summer dries out the timber, making it more flammable
Fire breaks out in a bakery in Pudding Lane on 2 September 1666
Strong winds push the flames westward through the crowded City
Firebreaks are delayed because building owners resist demolition
The Fire burns for days destroying around 13,000 houses and many churches

data.title: Order the chain for a typical witchcraft accusation
items: A neighbour refuses charity to a poor local woman
The poor woman speaks angrily against the household
Shortly after, a cow stops giving milk and a child falls ill
Neighbours connect these misfortunes to the woman's anger
Local fear and religious belief make the accusation seem credible
The woman is accused of witchcraft before local authorities
